I don't think it is a geological problem. Yes, people settled first were it was easiest to start a civilization but after that it is governments and economics that force where people live.

It all depends on politics and where/how to get the most GDP.
Grand Prairie (northwest of Edmonton) and Fort McMurray (northeast of Edmonton) are both 4.5 to 5 hour (in the boonies) from Edmonton, and both flourishing (for now) with a population of 60,000+. The reason? Oil and gas production. Oil and gas is for 25+% Alberta's GDP
Canada is not full and it is totally feasible to live on rock or further north in the boonies. But it's not economical. It is more economical (and for some cooler) to live in sky scrapers.
When I moved 3 decades ago from the Netherlands to Canada most of the urban expansion was  single household free standing homes. After a recession and covid, nowadays, single household houses are not profitable any more for developers. With the result that developers building multi household structures. And still, for the occupants it cost more than a free standing home 3 decades ago (even with the inflation conversion)

Maybe this is a nice fact: If Canada had the population density of the Netherlands. It would have a population of over 4 billion. Or half the global population.
